title: Sorting Algorithms
tagline: Five classic sorting algorithms, their complexity trade-offs, and why choosing the right one still matters in production code.

sections.content:
Sorting is arguably the most-studied problem in computer science — and for good reason. It appears everywhere: databases rank query results, search engines prioritise pages, operating systems schedule processes, and almost every algorithm that benefits from binary search first needs its input sorted. The problem statement is deceptively simple: given a list of elements, rearrange them in a defined order. Yet the question of *how* to do it efficiently reveals deep ideas about divide-and-conquer, recursion, memory hierarchies, and the limits of comparison-based computation.

The most important fact about sorting complexity is the **comparison-based lower bound**: any algorithm that sorts by comparing pairs of elements must perform at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. This is not a failing of our imagination — it is provable by information theory. There are n! possible orderings of n elements; each comparison eliminates roughly half the remaining possibilities; therefore at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons are unavoidable. Merge sort and quicksort both achieve this bound, making them asymptotically optimal among comparison sorts.

Five algorithms cover the full conceptual landscape. **Bubble sort** and **selection sort** are O(n²) and exist mainly for teaching. **Insertion sort** is also O(n²) worst-case but becomes O(n) on nearly-sorted input — a property that production systems actively exploit. **Merge sort** guarantees O(n log n) with stability and predictable memory use. **Quicksort** achieves O(n log n) on average with tiny constants and in-place operation, at the cost of an O(n²) worst case that randomisation nearly eliminates. Real-world runtimes like JavaScript's V8 use **TimSort** — a sophisticated merge sort / insertion sort hybrid — giving O(n log n) worst-case, O(n) best-case, and full stability.

This chapter builds each algorithm from scratch, explains *why* the complexity is what it is, shows real code you can run, covers the edge cases and misconceptions that trip up even experienced engineers, and ends with a guide on how to choose the right sort for any production scenario.

sections.title: Sorting a Hand of Playing Cards — Four Ways
sections.content:
Imagine you are dealt seven cards face-down and flip them one by one. As each card appears, you slide it leftward into the correct position among the cards already in your hand. You are doing **insertion sort** — natural, efficient when the hand is nearly ordered, but slow if the deck is completely random because each new card may have to travel all the way to the left edge.

Now picture a different player: before inserting anything, they scan all remaining cards to find the lowest one, place it first, then repeat — always hunting for the minimum. That is **selection sort**. It never does more than n swaps, but it always scans the entire unsorted portion even if the data is already perfect, so it cannot exploit pre-existing order.

**Bubble sort** is the friend who repeatedly passes through the hand, swapping any two adjacent out-of-order cards. The highest card keeps bubbling rightward until it reaches its final seat. It is simple to explain and simple to code, but the constant back-and-forth comparison makes it slower than insertion sort in practice.

**Merge sort** introduces a different strategy: split the deck in half, hand each half to a friend, let them sort independently, then merge the two sorted halves by comparing top cards and picking the smaller one each time. The splitting recurses until each sub-hand has one card (trivially sorted), then all the merges happen bottom-up. No matter how disordered the initial deck, the number of splits is always log₂(n) and each merge level processes all n cards — giving O(n log n) every time.

**Quicksort** is the most intuitive partition approach: pick one card as a pivot, move every smaller card to the left and every larger card to the right (without worrying about their order within each group), then recursively sort each group. On average the pivot splits the group roughly in half, giving O(n log n). But if you consistently pick the worst possible pivot — say, always the smallest card — every partition step only removes one element, and you are back to O(n²).

sections.title: Bubble Sort and Selection Sort — The O(n²) Baselines
sections.content:
**Bubble sort** works by making repeated passes through the array, comparing adjacent elements and swapping any that are out of order. After the first pass, the largest element has "bubbled" to the rightmost position. After the second pass, the second-largest is in position, and so on. With an **early-exit flag** — stopping if a complete pass produces zero swaps — bubble sort achieves O(n) best-case on already-sorted input. Without the flag it is always O(n²).

Why is it O(n²)? Consider the worst case: a reverse-sorted array. Every adjacent pair is out of order, so pass 1 makes n−1 swaps, pass 2 makes n−2, and so on. Total swaps = (n−1) + (n−2) + ... + 1 = n(n−1)/2, which is Θ(n²). Bubble sort is **stable**: equal elements never swap because the condition is strictly `arr[j] > arr[j+1]`, so equal elements pass each other without moving.

**Selection sort** scans the entire unsorted portion (from index `i` to `n−1`) to find the minimum element, then swaps it with the element at position `i`. It repeats this with `i` incrementing by 1 each time. The result is that each pass makes exactly **one swap** — so the total number of swaps is exactly n−1, regardless of the initial order.

This makes selection sort interesting when **writes are expensive** — for example, flash memory cells have a finite write lifetime. In that scenario, n−1 swaps versus potentially O(n²) swaps for bubble or insertion sort is meaningful. However, selection sort cannot detect an already-sorted array and always performs O(n²) comparisons. It is also **not stable** in the standard implementation: swapping a minimum element past equal elements disrupts their relative order.

**Insertion sort** is the most useful of the three O(n²) sorts. It maintains a sorted prefix and, for each new element, shifts larger elements in the sorted prefix one position to the right to create a slot, then inserts the new element. Think of it as maintaining a sorted hand of cards: as each new card arrives, you slide it leftward until it finds its correct position.

Insertion sort's superpower is **adaptive complexity**: the number of shifts is exactly the number of **inversions** (pairs of elements that are out of order) in the input. On a nearly-sorted array with only k inversions, insertion sort runs in O(n + k) time — which can be O(n) if k is small. This is why TimSort uses insertion sort for small sub-arrays: the overhead of recursive merge sort is not worth it for n < 32, and real-world data is often nearly-sorted in small windows.

sections.title: Merge Sort — Divide, Conquer, Merge
sections.content:
Merge sort is the classic **divide-and-conquer** sorting algorithm. It works on a recursive insight: if you have two already-sorted arrays, you can merge them into a single sorted array in O(n) time by repeatedly picking the smaller of the two front elements. The algorithm harnesses this by recursively sorting smaller and smaller sub-arrays until they reach size 1 (which is trivially sorted), then merging bottom-up.

**The recursion tree** is the key to understanding the complexity. At each level of recursion, the array is split in half. With n elements, there are log₂(n) levels before reaching single-element base cases. At every level, the merge step processes *all n elements* — each element is compared and moved exactly once per level. Total work = n elements × log n levels = **O(n log n)**, and this holds for every input — best, average, and worst case.

**Stability** is merge sort's defining advantage over quicksort. During the merge step, when `left[i] === right[j]`, we take the left element first (`left[i] <= right[j]`). This ensures that equal elements maintain their relative order from the original array. Stability is essential when you sort an array of objects by multiple keys: sort by secondary key first (stable), then by primary key (stable), and the secondary order is preserved within ties.

**Memory usage**: the merge step cannot be done in-place efficiently — it needs a temporary buffer to hold the merged result. At each recursion level, these buffers total O(n) space. This is merge sort's main drawback. An in-place merge sort exists but has poor constants. For most applications, O(n) extra space is acceptable, and the predictable O(n log n) time more than compensates.

**Bottom-up merge sort** is an iterative variant that avoids the recursion stack entirely. It starts by treating each element as a sorted sub-array of size 1, then repeatedly merges adjacent pairs of size 1 into size 2, size 2 into size 4, and so on. This is exactly what TimSort's merge phase does, with the added optimisation of detecting existing sorted "runs" and treating them as pre-sorted starting blocks.

sections.caption: Merge sort recursion tree: split until base cases (size 1), then merge bottom-up. Each merge level touches all n elements — O(n log n) total.

The `concat` after the while-loop handles the tail of whichever sub-array still has elements; exactly one of `left.slice(i)` or `right.slice(j)` will be non-empty. The final comment illustrates why O(n log n) vs O(n²) matters: at n=1,000,000 the difference is 25,000x in operation count.

sections.title: Quicksort — Pivot, Partition, Recurse
sections.content:
Quicksort is the algorithm that performance engineers reach for when they need the fastest in-practice sort. Despite sharing the O(n log n) average-case complexity with merge sort, quicksort typically outperforms it because of **cache locality**: the partition step accesses memory sequentially, making excellent use of CPU cache lines, whereas merge sort's merge step accesses two disjoint memory regions that may not both be in cache.

**The partition step** is the heart of quicksort. Choose one element as the **pivot** and rearrange the array so that all elements less than or equal to the pivot are to its left, and all elements greater are to its right. The pivot is then in its **final sorted position** and never needs to move again. Recurse on the left and right sub-arrays.

The **Lomuto partition scheme** (used in most textbook presentations) works by maintaining two pointers: `i` (the boundary of the "small" region) and `j` (the scan pointer). Whenever `arr[j] <= pivot`, we increment `i` and swap `arr[i]` with `arr[j]`. At the end, we swap the pivot (at `arr[hi]`) into position `i+1`. This is O(n) for a single partition.

**Why quicksort can be O(n²)**: the recursion depth equals the number of partition steps. In the best case, every pivot lands in the middle, the recursion tree has log n levels, and each level does O(n) work — O(n log n) total. In the worst case — when the pivot is always the minimum or maximum — every partition produces a sub-array of size n−1 and one of size 0. The recursion depth is n, giving O(n²).

**Random pivot selection** almost completely eliminates the worst case. The probability that all n pivots happen to be the minimum or maximum by chance is 1/n!, which is vanishingly small. Random pivot also defends against **adversarial inputs**: without randomisation, an attacker who knows your sorting implementation can craft a worst-case input and cause a Denial-of-Service (this is not theoretical — it has happened to web frameworks).

**Three-way partitioning** (Dutch National Flag algorithm by Dijkstra) handles duplicate values efficiently. Standard Lomuto treats all values equal to the pivot as "less than or equal," which can cause O(n²) behaviour on arrays with many duplicates. Three-way partitioning produces three regions — `< pivot`, `= pivot`, `> pivot` — and recurses only on the strictly lesser and greater regions, giving O(n) time on arrays of all identical elements.

**Stack depth**: each recursive call adds a frame. In the average case the recursion depth is O(log n). In the worst case it is O(n), which can cause a stack overflow for large n. The standard mitigation is **tail-call optimisation on the smaller partition**: always recurse on the smaller partition first (which is at most n/2), then loop on the larger. This bounds the stack depth to O(log n) regardless of pivot choice.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The random pivot swap to position `hi` is the key trick that makes Lomuto clean: the algorithm always treats `arr[hi]` as the pivot, so we just move any pivot there first. `i` starts at `lo - 1` (before the array) and only increments when we find an element that belongs in the left partition. After the loop, `arr[i+1]` through `arr[hi-1]` are all greater than the pivot, so swapping `arr[hi]` to `arr[i+1]` places the pivot in its correct final position.

sections.title: TimSort — The Algorithm Production Systems Use
sections.content:
JavaScript's `Array.prototype.sort`, Python's `sorted()`, and Java's `Arrays.sort()` for objects all use **TimSort**, invented by Tim Peters in 2002 for CPython. TimSort is a sophisticated merge sort / insertion sort hybrid that achieves the best of both worlds.

TimSort exploits a key observation about real-world data: **data is rarely uniformly random**. Files, database records, and user lists tend to have local ordering — partial runs of already-sorted elements. TimSort identifies these **natural runs** (maximal already-sorted sub-sequences, including reverse-sorted runs which are reversed in O(n)) and treats them as the leaves of its merge tree, rather than splitting all the way down to individual elements.

**The algorithm in outline**: (1) Scan left-to-right to find natural runs; if a run is shorter than the `minRun` threshold (~32–64 elements), extend it to `minRun` length using **insertion sort**. (2) Push runs onto a stack. (3) While the top of the stack violates the **merge invariants** (designed to keep the merge tree balanced), merge adjacent runs. (4) After the whole array has been scanned, merge remaining runs.

The merge invariants (A, B, C are stack run lengths) ensure `A > B + C` and `B > C`. This guarantees the tree has O(log n) height and that each element participates in O(log n) merges, giving O(n log n) worst-case. On already-sorted input, TimSort finds one long run and does zero merges — **O(n) best case**.

**Stability since ES2019**: ECMAScript 2019 mandated that `Array.prototype.sort` be stable. All major engines (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) had already implemented stable sort — V8 switched to TimSort in 2019, replacing an unstable algorithm it used for arrays larger than 10 elements. This means you can safely rely on `Array.sort` for multi-key sorting in modern JavaScript.

**The `minRun` threshold**: TimSort switches to insertion sort for runs shorter than `minRun` (typically 32–64). Insertion sort has lower overhead for small n because it avoids merge bookkeeping and accesses memory in a simple sequential pattern that CPUs prefetch well. The exact threshold is chosen so that the number of initial runs is always a power of two (or close to it), keeping the merge tree perfectly balanced.

sections.label: Concept
sections.explanation: The two-pass stable sort technique is a classic interview question: 'How do you sort by multiple keys?' The answer — stable sort by secondary key, then stable sort by primary key — only works when the sort is stable. JavaScript's Array.sort has been guaranteed stable since ES2019, making this pattern safe in modern JS.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis Deep Dive — Why O(n log n) is the Lower Bound
sections.content:
Every comparison-based sorting algorithm must use at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. This is proven through **decision tree analysis**. Model any deterministic comparison sort as a binary tree where each internal node is a comparison (is `a[i] < a[j]`?) and each leaf is a final sorted ordering. For n elements, there are n! possible orderings (permutations). Every leaf of the decision tree must correspond to at least one of these orderings, so the tree has at least n! leaves.

A binary tree with at least n! leaves must have depth at least log₂(n!) comparisons in the worst case (the worst-case path from root to leaf). By Stirling's approximation, log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂(n) − n log₂(e) ≈ n log₂(n). Therefore: **every comparison sort must make Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case**. Merge sort achieves this exactly — it is optimal.

**Non-comparison sorts can break the barrier**: algorithms like **counting sort** and **radix sort** do not compare elements directly. Counting sort works when elements are integers in a known range [0, k]: it counts occurrences, then reconstructs the sorted array. Time complexity O(n + k), space O(k). When k = O(n), this is O(n) — linear! Radix sort sorts integers digit-by-digit using a stable counting sort on each digit. Time O(d(n + k)) where d is the number of digits. For 32-bit integers with base 256, d=4, k=256 — effectively O(n) for practical integer sizes.

The catch: these linear-time sorts only work on specific data types (integers with bounded range, or strings with bounded alphabet). For general comparable objects — the most common use case — comparison sorts are the only option, and Ω(n log n) is unavoidable.

**Practical constant factors matter enormously**: O(n log n) hides a constant. Merge sort, quicksort, and heapsort all have the same asymptotic bound, but in practice quicksort is typically 2–3x faster than heapsort and somewhat faster than merge sort for random data, because its access patterns are more cache-friendly. For n up to a few hundred, insertion sort's O(n²) with a small constant beats merge sort's O(n log n) with its recursion overhead — which is precisely why TimSort uses a hybrid approach.

sections.title: Common Misconceptions and Edge Cases
sections.content:
**'Quicksort is always faster than merge sort'**: Quicksort wins on random data in practice, but merge sort wins on nearly-sorted data, on linked lists (where random access is O(n)), and when stability is required. The real answer is 'it depends on input characteristics and hardware.'

**'The worst case for quicksort is rare'**: Without random pivot selection, it is not rare at all — it occurs on already-sorted arrays, reverse-sorted arrays, and arrays with many duplicates. These are extremely common in practice. Always use random pivot or median-of-three. Web frameworks have been attacked via hash-table DoS (related) and sort DoS because of fixed-pivot quicksort.

**'Merge sort uses O(n log n) space'**: No — it uses O(n) space. At any given moment, the merge step only needs O(n) total buffer space across all active merge calls at a single recursion level. The recursion stack adds O(log n) frames, but each frame just stores indices — negligible. Total: O(n).

**'Stable means faster'**: Stability is a correctness property, not a performance one. A sort is stable if equal elements keep their relative order. Stability has zero effect on speed.

**'Array.sort in JavaScript is stable'**: This is **true since ES2019**, but was false in older engines. V8 (Chrome/Node) was unstable for arrays longer than 10 elements before 2019. If you maintain code that must run in very old environments, verify.

**Handling duplicate elements**: Standard quicksort can degrade to O(n²) on arrays where all elements are identical, because every partition puts all elements on one side. Three-way partitioning (Dutch National Flag) solves this by creating a `= pivot` region in the middle that is not recursed into, giving O(n) time on uniform arrays.

**Off-by-one errors in partition**: The Lomuto scheme's `i = lo - 1` and the loop `j` from `lo` to `hi - 1` (exclusive) are specific. Getting `hi` vs `hi - 1` wrong causes either an infinite loop or an unsorted result. The Hoare partition scheme (the original) uses two inward-moving pointers and is slightly more efficient but trickier to get right.

**Historical context worth knowing**: Merge sort was invented by John von Neumann in 1945, making it one of the oldest algorithms still in ubiquitous use. Quicksort was invented by Tony Hoare in 1959 (published 1962) and was a breakthrough: its in-place partitioning and cache-friendly access patterns made it far faster in practice than anything available at the time. Hoare called it quicksort because it was genuinely quick. TimSort, invented by Tim Peters in 2002, introduced the natural-run detection idea that made it dramatically faster on real-world (partially ordered) data. The ECMAScript 2019 specification finally mandated stable sort, 30 years after JavaScript was invented — reflecting how long it took for hardware and engine optimisations to make stable sort practical at all input sizes.

**Interview and production traps to know cold**: (1) 'What is the worst case of quicksort?' — O(n²), triggered by sorted input with fixed pivot; mitigated by random pivot. (2) 'When is insertion sort better than merge sort?' — Small n (less than ~32) and nearly-sorted data; O(n) on sorted input. (3) 'How do you sort by multiple keys in JavaScript?' — Two-pass stable sort: secondary key first, primary key second; relies on Array.sort being stable (ES2019+). (4) 'Why is merge sort preferred for linked lists?' — Linked lists have O(n) random access; merge sort never needs random access (it always processes contiguous runs or follows next-pointers); quicksort's partitioning requires random access. (5) 'Can you sort in O(n)?' — Yes, with counting sort or radix sort, but only for integers with bounded range — the comparison-sort lower bound is Ω(n log n) and is provably unavoidable for general data.

items: **Bubble, selection, and insertion sort** are O(n²) — fine for n < 20 or nearly-sorted data (insertion sort is O(n) on sorted input), but catastrophically slow at scale.
**Merge sort** guarantees O(n log n) in all cases and is stable; it costs O(n) auxiliary space and is the right choice when stability is non-negotiable or input may be adversarial.
**Quicksort** is O(n log n) average with excellent cache performance and O(1) extra space; it is not stable and degrades to O(n²) without random pivot selection — always randomise.

The **Ω(n log n) lower bound** is provable by decision tree analysis — no comparison-based sort can do better in the worst case; counting sort and radix sort beat it only for integer data with bounded range.

**Stability** means equal elements preserve their original relative order; it enables the two-pass multi-key sort pattern and is essential for database-style ordering; JavaScript's Array.sort has been guaranteed stable since ES2019.

**TimSort** (used by JavaScript, Python, Java) detects natural sorted runs, extends short ones with insertion sort, then merges using balanced stack invariants — achieving O(n) on nearly-sorted data and O(n log n) worst-case.

In production, **prefer Array.sort** (or the language's built-in) unless you have a specific reason not to — it is highly optimised, stable, and well-tested; understand the algorithms to reason about edge cases, not to re-implement them.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort, and why does it never degrade below this?
options: O(n²) — it depends on the initial order of elements
O(n log n) — it always splits into halves and each merge level processes all n elements
O(n) — it detects sorted runs and skips unnecessary work
O(n log n) average but O(n²) if the array is reverse-sorted
quiz.explanation: Merge sort's recursion always halves the array (log n levels) regardless of input order, and each level's merge step processes all n elements — O(n) per level. This gives O(n log n) in best, average, and worst cases. Unlike quicksort, merge sort has no 'unlucky' input that causes degeneration.

quiz.question: Which sorting algorithm is NOT stable in its standard implementation?
options: Bubble sort
Insertion sort
Merge sort
Selection sort
quiz.explanation: Selection sort swaps the found minimum into position, which can jump it over equal elements — disrupting their relative order. Bubble sort uses strict `>` comparison so equal elements never swap (stable). Insertion sort shifts elements only when strictly greater (stable). Merge sort uses `<=` in the merge step (stable).

quiz.question: Why does quicksort use random pivot selection rather than always picking the first or last element?
options: Random pivot makes quicksort stable
Random pivot reduces auxiliary space from O(n) to O(log n)
Fixed-pivot quicksort degrades to O(n²) on sorted input, which is common in practice and exploitable by attackers
Random pivot guarantees O(n log n) worst case
quiz.explanation: With a fixed first/last-element pivot, any already-sorted or reverse-sorted array causes every partition to be maximally unbalanced — O(n²). This is not a rare edge case; sorted and nearly-sorted arrays are extremely common in practice. Adversarial inputs can also deliberately trigger this. Random pivot makes the worst case astronomically unlikely. It does not make quicksort stable or guarantee O(n log n) worst-case (that remains O(n²) in theory, just negligibly rare).

quiz.question: On which type of input does insertion sort outperform merge sort in practice?
options: Large random arrays of one million elements
Reverse-sorted arrays of any size
Nearly-sorted arrays and very small arrays (n < 32)
Arrays with a large number of duplicates
quiz.explanation: Insertion sort is O(n + k) where k is the number of inversions. On nearly-sorted data, k is small and insertion sort approaches O(n). For small n, insertion sort's tiny constant factor and sequential cache access beats merge sort's recursion and slice overhead. TimSort exploits both properties: it uses insertion sort to extend short runs and for sub-arrays below ~32 elements.

quiz.question: What auxiliary space does merge sort require, and why?
options: O(1) — it sorts in-place using swaps
O(log n) — only the recursion stack frames
O(n) — the merge step needs a temporary buffer to combine two sorted halves
O(n log n) — one buffer per recursion level
quiz.explanation: The merge step cannot be done in-place without prohibitive complexity. It reads from two sorted sub-arrays and writes into a separate buffer, which at each level totals O(n) across all active merges. The recursion stack adds O(log n) frames, but each is small. Total is O(n) — not O(n log n), because different recursion levels reuse the same buffer space.

quiz.question: What is TimSort (used by JavaScript's Array.sort since ES2019)?
options: A time-limited variant of bubble sort that terminates after a fixed number of passes
A hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort that detects natural sorted runs and achieves O(n) on nearly-sorted data
Quicksort with three-way partitioning and median-of-three pivot selection
A parallel sorting algorithm that distributes work across multiple CPU cores
quiz.explanation: TimSort scans for natural sorted runs, extends short runs with insertion sort to a minimum length, then merges runs using stack-invariant-based merge sort. On already-sorted or nearly-sorted data it finds long runs and does minimal merging — O(n). Worst-case is O(n log n). It is stable and guaranteed by ECMAScript 2019.

quiz.question: You need to sort an array of 1 million employee records first by department, then by salary within each department. Which approach is correct?
options: Sort by department first using a stable sort, then by salary using any sort
Sort by salary first using a stable sort, then by department using a stable sort
Sort by both keys simultaneously using a single comparator that checks department then salary
Use quicksort twice — first by department, then by salary
quiz.explanation: The two-pass stable sort technique: sort by the secondary key (salary) first with a stable sort, then sort by the primary key (department) with a stable sort. Stability ensures that within each department group after the second pass, the salary order from the first pass is preserved. Options A and D are wrong order; option C also works (single comparator) but the question is about the two-pass technique specifically; option B is the correct two-pass approach.

quiz.question: What is the best-case time complexity of bubble sort WITH the early-exit optimisation?
options: O(n²) — bubble sort is always quadratic
O(n log n) — it becomes like merge sort on sorted input
O(n) — one pass with no swaps detects an already-sorted array
O(1) — it immediately detects the sorted condition
quiz.explanation: With the early-exit flag: if a complete pass produces zero swaps, the array is sorted and the algorithm terminates. On an already-sorted array, exactly one pass of n−1 comparisons occurs — O(n). Without the flag, bubble sort always does all n(n−1)/2 comparisons regardless of input — O(n²).

quiz.question: What is the theoretical lower bound on the number of comparisons any comparison-based sorting algorithm must make in the worst case?
options: O(n) — by scanning once you can determine the sorted order
O(n log n) — proven via decision tree analysis: there are n! orderings requiring at least log₂(n!) comparisons
O(n²) — you must compare every pair of elements
There is no lower bound; clever algorithms can sort in O(1)
quiz.explanation: By decision tree analysis: any deterministic comparison sort can be modelled as a binary decision tree with at least n! leaves (one per permutation). A binary tree with n! leaves has depth at least log₂(n!) ≈ n log n by Stirling's approximation. Therefore Ω(n log n) comparisons are unavoidable. This is a proven lower bound — not just a property of known algorithms. Counting/radix sort escape it by not using comparisons.

quiz.question: What is the space complexity of quicksort's call stack in the WORST case, and how is it mitigated?
options: O(log n) in all cases — recursion is always balanced
O(n) worst case when pivot is always min/max; mitigated by always recursing on the smaller partition first
O(n²) — one stack frame per comparison
O(1) — quicksort is fully in-place including the call stack
quiz.explanation: In the worst case (pivot always smallest/largest), recursion depth is O(n) — one level per element — risking a stack overflow for large n. The standard mitigation: always recurse on the smaller partition first (which is at most n/2 elements) and either loop or tail-recurse on the larger. This guarantees the recursion depth never exceeds O(log n) regardless of pivot quality. Average case is O(log n) naturally.
